Bounce, Move, Return! Building Coordination & Confidence Through Pickleball Part 2

by Jordan Aaron Weber

Print this article

Article URL: https://www.parentingspecialneeds.org/article/bounce-move-return-building-coordination-confidence-through-pickleball-part-2/

Pickleball For Every Ability • Part 2

 

Advertisement:

 

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:11
Instaread

New to the series? Start with Part 1: Grab a paddle! Beginner Pickleball Skills for Players of All Abilities

The highlighted pink links in the article are links to video demonstrations.

 

Lesson 2: Intermediate Pickleball Skills

Part 2 builds on the beginner paddle skills from Part 1 and brings them closer to the court. Players practice moving, watching the ball, and controlling the paddle. These three activities build footwork, agility, reaction time, ball control, and spatial awareness. Choose the version that helps your player feel successful, and celebrate each small gain.

 

Skill 1 — 4-Cone Agility & N Agility Drill

Equipment needed: Four cones, a pickleball paddle, and an optional timer. Set four cones in a square. Keep the paddle in hand as the player moves. Try each pattern five times. A timer can make the activity fun, but smooth movement matters more than speed.

 

Box Drill

Start at one corner. Move forward to the next cone, side-step to the third cone, move backward to the fourth cone, then side-step back to the start.

 

 

Box Drill: Move forward, side-step, move backward, and side-step home.

N Drill

Start at a corner. Run toward to the cone in front of you followed by the cone diagonal from you, followed by the cone in front of you. Athletes can backpedal or run in a curved pathway around the first cone after the start.

 

 

N Drill: Follow a forward–diagonal–forward path.

 

Try it: Make the path smaller for an easier course. Players can walk, side-step, skip, hop, gallop, bear crawl, or crab walk the pattern. Add a center cone for a star shaped path.

 

Skill 2-Ball Control

Equipment needed: A pickleball paddle and a wiffle ball, pickleball, foam ball, or balloon.

 

Part A — Keep it Up (Juggling)

Use an underhand motion to tap the ball upward from the paddle. Start while standing still, then add a few small steps. This practices the
same upward motion used to return a ball.

Count how many taps the player can make in 10, 20, or 30 seconds.
See how quickly the player can juggle 10, 20, or 30 taps.
When ready, try a few steps forward, backward, or side to side.

 

 

Keep It Up: Start in one spot, then add gentle movement.

 

Part B — Ground Bounce

Bounce the ball off the ground withe paddle repeatedly – stationary then moving Build downward paddle control and ball trajectory reading.

Timed Challenges:

Advertisement:

Try 10, 20, or 30 seconds
Count how quickly the player can make 10, 20, or 30 bounces.
When ready, take a few steps while keeping the bounce under
control.

Ground Bounce: Use gentle downward taps to keep the ball close.

 

Skill 3 —  Keep it Up Balloon Game

Equipment needed: A pickleball paddle and a balloon. Use an indoor or nonwindy space.

Use the paddle to keep a balloon in the air as long as possible. Players can play alone or with a partner. A balloon moves slowly, giving the player more time to watch, move, and make a successful return.

Cues: Verbal: “Watch the balloon.” “Move your feet or body to get under it.”
Tactile: Tap the players shoulder to indicate which side to use.

Challenges:

Count how many touches the player makes before the balloon drops.
Try 10 forehands, and then 10 backhands.
Alternate sides each time,
Alternate hands (go from right to left hand)

 

 

Keep It Up with a balloon: A slower, high-success option for solo or partner play.

 

Coaches’ Insight: These activities show how a player moves, changes direction, controls the ball, and responds to cues. They also build continuous repetitions of footwork, hand-eye coordination, balance, and focus.

Adapt It: Shrink the agility pattern or remove direction changes for a simpler forward-and-back path. A securely hung soft ball at paddle height, set up and supervised by an adult, can give steady practice without chasing the ball.

Parent Coaching Tip: Do the activity first and let your player follow your movements. Model one direction at a time, then step back and let them try. For Coaches and Teachers: Keep the games fun and active. Short, repeated turns help players practice coordination, agility, balance, and focus without feeling overwhelmed.

Encouragement for Parents: Count volleys out loud. Cheer when the ball stays up. Let your child decide when to start again. You do not need to fix every mistake; one encouraging cue is worth more than five corrections. If they are smiling, it is working.

Try This Game — Agility King of the Court: One player moves through the 4-cone pattern while another player times them. Write down the time, switch roles, and choose a new movement for the next round. Play against your own time, not against each other

 

About Our Expert

Jordan Aaron Weber

Assistant Professor – Healthful Living and Fitness Education

Dr. Jordan Aaron Weber is an Associate Professor of Healthful Living and Fitness Education at UNC Wilmington, with over 20 years of experience in physical education and adapted activity. He is passionate about helping individuals build lifelong movement skills that support both physical and emotional well-being.
